rows.question: I bought a flat and the builder has not handed over possession on time. Can I go to the consumer court and also ask for my money back under the real estate law?
queries: I bought a flat and the builder has not handed over possession on time. Can I go to the consumer court and also ask for my money back under the real estate law?
builder delay in handing over possession refund and compensation
Consumer Protection Act 2019 complaint by flat purchaser housing service deficiency
Real Estate Regulation and Development Act 2016 return of amount and compensation section 18
topSources: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016. s18

rows.answer:
The failure of the developer to hand over possession within the contractually stipulated period amounts to a deficiency of service under Section 2(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and a consumer is not bound to accept possession after an inordinate delay and can seek a refund of the amount deposited with interest, as seen in the Supreme Court judgments in Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. versus Govindan Raghavan [11], Experion Developers Pvt. Ltd. versus Sushma Ashok Shiroor [12], and Wg. Cdr. Arifur Rahman Khan and Aleya Sultana and Ors. versus DLF Southern Homes Pvt. Ltd. and Ors. [13].

Under Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, if the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment, plot, or building in accordance with the agreement for sale or due to discontinuance of business, the promoter shall be liable on demand to the allottees, in case the allottee wishes to withdraw from the project, to return the amount received with interest at such rate as may be prescribed and compensation [1].

rows.question: Is a gift of a house to my daughter valid if it is only written on plain paper, and does it need registration?
queries: Is a gift of a house to my daughter valid if it is only written on plain paper, and does it need registration?
gift of immovable property transfer of property plain paper validity
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 section 122 gift of immovable property
The Registration Act, 1908 section 17 documents of which registration is compulsory
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s122
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s123
rows.answer:
A gift of immovable property such as a house cannot be effected without a registered instrument, so a gift written only on plain paper is not valid and registration is required under Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 [2][3][11].

Conditions and time limits:
- The transfer for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses, as provided in Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [3].
- The acceptance of the gift must be made during the lifetime of the donor and while the donor is still capable of giving, according to Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 18 of the Registration Act, 1908 sets out documents of which registration is optional [4].

Regarding relevant Supreme Court judgments, the excerpt from the Supreme Court judgment in "Hafeeza Bibi & Ors. versus Shaikh Farid (Dead) by Lrs. & Ors." notes that a deed of gift executed by a Mohammadan is not the instrument effecting the gift but a mere piece of evidence [10]. rows.answer:
The District Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees under Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 [8]. The Supreme Court judgment in "U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. and Ors. versus Anis Ahmed" notes that a complaint may be made when goods bought suffer from one or more defects [11].

Conditions and time limits:
- The complaint may be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the opposite party resides or carries on business or has a branch office, the cause of action wholly or in part arises, or the complainant resides or personally works for gain under Section 34 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 [8].

rows.question: What does section 111 of the BNS say about organised crime, and was there such a section in the IPC?
queries: What does section 111 of the BNS say about organised crime, and was there such a section in the IPC?
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 111 punishment for organised crime
Indian Penal Code corresponding provision to organised crime section 111 BNS
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 s484
rows.answer:
Organised crime is defined as any continuing unlawful activity including kidnapping, robbery, vehicle theft, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offence, cyber-crimes, trafficking of persons, drugs, weapons or illicit goods or services, human trafficking for prostitution or ransom, by any person or a group of persons acting in concert, singly or jointly, as a member of an organised crime syndicate or on behalf of such syndicate, by use of violence, threat of violence, intimidation, coercion, or by any other unlawful means to obtain direct or indirect material benefit including a financial benefit, under Section 111 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

There was no such section in the Indian Penal Code, 1860; Section 4 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 states that the new offence of organised crime has been added in the Bill with deterrent punishments to deal effectively with the problem of organised crimes [1][2].

The old law this replaced: section 53 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Punishments) [6].

rows.answer:
Under the old law, every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, was required to be reduced to writing by him or under his direction and read over to the informant, and every such information whether given in writing or reduced to writing was signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof was entered in a prescribed book under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [8].

The current law that covers this is Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [1][8].

Conditions and time limits:
- Information may be given orally or by electronic communication to an officer in charge of a police station [1].
- Oral information must be reduced to writing and read over to the informant, and signed by the person giving it [1].
- Information given by electronic communication must be signed within three days by the person giving it [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 175 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 covers "Police officer's power to investigate cognizable case" [5].

rows.question: What is the BNS offence of causing death by negligence, and which IPC section was it earlier?
queries: What is the BNS offence of causing death by negligence, and which IPC section was it earlier?
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 106 causing death by negligence
Indian Penal Code section 304A causing death by negligence
causing death by negligence rash or negligent act
topSources: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 s531
rows.answer:
The offence of causing death by negligence under Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, applies to whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide [1]. This provision replaced Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, which is the old law [8].

Conditions and time limits:
- If the act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing a medical procedure, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term up to two years, with fine [1].
- If the act is done by rash and negligent driving of a vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and the offender escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term up to ten years, with fine [1].
- In all other cases, the punishment is imprisonment of either description for a term up to five years, with fine [1].

rows.question: How do I prove an email as evidence in court under the Evidence Act section 65B?
queries: How do I prove an email as evidence in court under the Evidence Act section 65B?

Indian Evidence Act section 65B admissibility of electronic record certificate
topSources: The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, 1 of 1872 (Rep., Act 47 of 2023) s65B
rows.answer:
Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 is the current law in force from 1 July 2024; it replaced Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 [5].

To give a statement from an electronic record in evidence under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, a certificate must be submitted along with the electronic record at each instance where it is being submitted for admission [1]. The certificate must identify the electronic record containing the statement and describe the manner in which it was produced, give particulars of any device involved in its production to show it was produced by a computer or communication device, and deal with the matters to which the conditions relating to computer output relate [1]. The certificate must purport to be signed by a person in charge of the computer or communication device or the management of the relevant activities, and it shall be evidence of any matter stated in the certificate to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person stating it [1].

Every police officer or other person making an arrest under the Sanhita must forthwith give information regarding the arrest and the place where the arrested person is being held to any of the arrested person's relatives, friends, or other nominated persons, under Section 48 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced Section 50A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) [3][9].

- Within six hours: The time limit for a private person who makes an arrest to hand the arrested person over to a police officer or take them to the nearest police station, under Section 40 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [5].

rows.question: My son took over my house and now ignores me and my wife. Can we cancel the transfer?
queries: My son took over my house and now ignores me and my wife. Can we cancel the transfer?

rows.answer:
The transfer of property can be declared void by the Tribunal at the option of the transferor under Section 23 of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 [1].

Conditions and time limits:
- The property must have been transferred by a senior citizen by way of gift or otherwise after the commencement of the Act [1].
- The transfer must have been made subject to the condition that the transferee shall provide the basic amenities and basic physical needs to the transferor [1][11].
- The transferee must have refused or failed to provide such amenities and physical needs [1][11].

In Urmila Dixit versus Sunil Sharan Dixit and Ors., the Supreme Court noted that Section 23(1) requires the transfer to be subject to the condition of providing basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee's refusal or failure to provide them [11].

rows.question: Someone made a fake profile with my photos to cheat my friends. What can I do?
queries: Someone made a fake profile with my photos to cheat my friends. What can I do?

Information Technology Act 2000 section 66D punishment for cheating by personation using computer resource
topSources: The INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000 Amendment s66D
The Information Technology Act, 2000 (Central Act 21 of 2000) s66D
rows.answer:
For cheating by personation by using a computer resource, you can be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to one lakh rupees under Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [2][4][5]. For identity theft by fraudulently or dishonestly making use of the unique identification feature or password of another person, you can be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to rupees one lakh under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1][7][8]. Furthermore, under Section 319 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced section 419 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the old law), whoever cheats by personation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both [3].

Whoever intends to insult the modesty of a woman by uttering any words, making any sound or gesture, or exhibiting any object, or intruding upon her privacy, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term extending up to three years and also with fine under Section 79 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 509 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 [1][8].

Conditions and time limits:
- Information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence may be given orally or by electronic communication to an officer in charge of a police station under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [2][9].
- If information is given orally, it must be reduced to writing, read over to the informant, and signed by the person giving it under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [2].
- If information is given by electronic communication, it must be taken on record and signed within three days by the person giving it under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 [2].
